title: Divorce, smartphones and control - BBC sees how Taliban run Afghanistan
description: Figure caption, Watch: Eighteen-year-old woman argues her case for a divorce, saying her "honour and dignity have already been ruined"ByKawoon Khamoos
body: Figure caption, Watch: Eighteen-year-old woman argues her case for a divorce, saying her "honour and dignity have already been ruined"ByKawoon KhamooshBBC World ServiceReporting fromSheberghan, Kabul and KandaharGovernor Abdullah Sarhadi gives money to treat a boy's broken arm and hands out funds for a local mosque - then, in his office in northern Afghanistan, an astonishing exchange unfolds.A young woman tells the grey-bearded former Taliban commander that she wants to divorce her husband, who she accuses of months of abuse and beatings.She will not take no for an answer.In a country where girls are banned from secondary education, the 18-year-old argues her case calmly and confidently, her face completely hidden behind a full-face veil and sunglasses."If there was any chance to live together, I wouldn't be here… I have taken my decision," she says.After trying to persuade her to avoid divorce, the governor later comments that women are "mindless" and "deficient in intellect", to laughter from the male officials, bodyguards and elders around him.The moment gives a rare glimpse into the day-to-day realities of the Taliban's rule, five years after they swept aside the US-backed government in 2021.Image caption, The governor of Jawzjan province, Abdullah Sarhadi, who fought for the Taliban was held in US detention in Guantanamo Bay for several years In that time, women have been excluded from most workplaces, banned from universities and may not travel alone or visit parks and leisure centres.In encounters spread over two years, the BBC gained unusual access to influential figures in the extreme Islamist movement, spending time with men who once planned suicide attacks or spent years in underground hideouts, but are now officials and soldiers.The Taliban came into power saying they had changed, but many of their policies are similar to the hard-line interpretation of Sharia - Islamic religious law - they imposed in the 1990s.The men we met seemed to want to present themselves as reasonable, yet were not keen to discuss their past violence. And we saw moments of unease between the rulers and those they rule.Governor Sarhadi says Tuba – not her real name – should stay in the marriage."Ask yourself: 'Who would marry me after I get my divorce?'" says Sarhadi. "You'll have to compromise a lot or you'll lose your dignity and honour.""Mr Governor, my honour and dignity have already been ruined," she responds.Her husband listens, awaiting his turn to speak.Under Sharia, a woman requesting that her husband agrees to a divorce may have to return some or all of the money given to her by him when they married. A financial settlement is often agreed. But this woman's husband says he wants four times the amount, which her family refuses to pay.The governor says the woman should be given her own room. He adds that officials will warn him not to beat her - "otherwise he'd be jailed".Unsatisfied, Tuba's father later tells the BBC the family will pursue divorce through the courts, even though, under the Taliban's court system, it is very difficult for a woman to get a divorce without the husband's consent.Image source, EPA/REX/ShutterstockImage caption, A hole left by the destruction of one of the Buddha statues in Bamiyan -  Sarhadi says he destroyed itSarhadi was a military commander during the Taliban's first stint in power in the 1990s. He was among thousands of insurgents who surrendered in late 2001 as a US-led coalition ousted the group.He was held for several years in US detention in Guantanamo Bay, but eventually released.When the Taliban regained power, he became a governor - first in the province of Bamiyan, then when we met him in late June, in Sheberghan city in Jawzjan province. He has recently become deputy commander of a military corps in the northern province of Kunduz.Tapping on an old-style mobile with a tiny screen, he says a recent ban on smartphones for officials has slowed things down. "Before, you could send a quick message… sending documents and getting an answer fast." If he says any more about the ban, "it will cause trouble", he adds.But in other ways his worldview seems largely unchanged from the Taliban's position 25 years ago. Then, he was a military commander in Bamiyan, where the Taliban blew up ancient giant Buddha statues, triggering international shock and condemnation.He initially tries to avoid our questions about the archaeological site, but eventually, he says: "I destroyed it with my own hands."Whatever we did and we do is in accordance with the guidance and God's law… We smash idols rather than sell them. Why should I regret? It was God's will."In the capital Kabul, we meet another senior Taliban figure who swapped a violent past for a role with the ruling administration.Habibullah Badr drives us through the streets in an armoured car.He says he was previously "responsible for the operations of suicide attackers" in Kabul."I know all the roads and streets very well… we had all the information we needed about Kabul and its alleys," he says. "There were areas that needed a long time to plan."Taliban suicide attacks killed thousands of people in Afghanistan, including many civilians.Badr is cautious about discussing his past though, fearing it will "make people upset" and could "reopen wounds".Asked about civilian deaths, he says the Taliban targeted US convoys and that civilians were urged to stay away from foreign bases.Whenever I try to ask him about specific attacks that took place in civilian areas, he evades the question.Image caption, Habibullah Badr says that in the past he was involved in operations involving suicide attacksHe is currently taking time out from official roles for medical treatment, but was previously deputy head of prisons for the whole country – and ran the very jail where he was held on death row under the previous government.Badr invites us to join him at a tribal gathering, where the head of a charitable foundation is to honour him with a medal. But things take an unexpected turn."Mr Badr is a pride for Afghanistan and a great fighter," says Sultan Mohammad Talaee. "But I also have a complaint. If the schools and education were open to all it would be a great work for Afghanistan. I hope this doesn't offend you."An awkward silence follows, his audience unsure how to react. Talaee's microphone is swiftly removed.Afterwards, he tells the BBC: "I requested for the girls' schools to reopen… seeking knowledge is an obligation for both men and women in Islam."He adds: "There were other things I wanted to say but they didn't let me talk more."The Taliban: Coming Out of the ShadowsAudiences in the UK can watch on iPlayer from 17:00 and on Global Eye on BBC Two at 19:00Often those who speak out face much more severe consequences.Women told us of the deep despair they felt over dreams thwarted by restrictions on education, and of friends jailed for protesting.Most journalists we spoke to said they had been summoned or questioned by the Taliban's intelligence organisation, Estikhbaraat.The BBC put some of these concerns to the Taliban government's spokesman, known as Zabihullah Mujahid.Image caption, Zabihullah Mujahid says women's rights and freedom of speech need to be seen "through the Sharia lens"He has been a public face for the Taliban government since 2021. He still uses the pseudonym he went by for years during the insurgency, but he told us his real name is Tahir Shah Seddiqi - revealing it publicly for the first time.In a lavish press centre funded by the Americans for the previous government, we ask him about the first press conference he gave there, two days after the Taliban took control of the country.Then, he told the world the Taliban government would allow women to work and study "within our frameworks" and they would "be very active" in society. Why did they fail to keep their word?"We are committed to women's rights, freedom of speech and other things within Sharia," he replies. "We should see everything through the Sharia lens."Allowing women to work in offices such as his own "would lead to immoralities" and "their dignity would be undermined", he adds.He says the issue of education for women is "under discussions… we need a Sharia-based solution for it".When questioned about the Taliban's crackdown on media freedom, he says: "In a society like Afghanistan we have our restrictions. We can't let media do whatever propaganda they want… they can't broadcast against Islamic laws and rites."The Taliban government sits in Kabul, but Mujahid spends a lot of time in the southern city of Kandahar, the Taliban's heartland, which some now consider the de facto capital.We ask to meet the Taliban's supreme leader, Hibatullah Akhundzada, who is based there. He rarely appears in public and has never given a media interview - we are told it will not be possible at the moment.Restrictions have been tightened in Kandahar since I last visited two years ago. Now men must have beards. Radio stations are not allowed to play music or broadcast women's voices, and we were not allowed to film in the city.Two hours' drive away, along dusty roads, some of the group's most devoted former fighters showed the BBC the insurgents' old secret cave network.Abid Lalai, a former fighter who now mans a checkpoint as part of a security force under the interior ministry, shows us the holes he fired from and the places he used to put his Quran and hang AK-47s.Image caption, Abid Lalai is one of many Taliban fighters who hid out in caves to evade capture under previous governmentsHis superior, Abdul Samad, shows us an unmarked graveyard, saying his father is buried here, killed fighting for the Taliban.The area is one of the most deprived in a country where the UN says three in four people cannot provide for their basic needs. Samad says the local population desperately need water, roads and clinics."Emirate [Taliban] officials have not forgotten us," says Samad. He says the leaders may be busy with other priorities. "We are hopeful, they will look after us sometime."Five years since the Taliban began their second stint in power, poverty, unemployment and economic instability remain pressing concerns.Taliban figures we spoke to said they were working to tackle them, but we met other people who believe the group itself is the country's main problem."I'm speechless about how a group that has no understanding about life is suddenly in power," says Hoda - not her real name - a woman who protested on the streets when the Taliban first returned to power."Women can't accept this situation," she tells the BBC. "They might advance restrictions but it won't stay like this forever.""I think the Taliban are scared of educated women," she adds. "That's why they restrict women. They want uneducated women so they can't raise wise men. Because that would end the Taliban."Additional reporting by Hafizullah Maroof

schema.headline: Divorce, smartphones and control - BBC sees how Taliban run Afghanistan

title: Sharing dangerous driving videos is 'truly reprehensible', PM says
description: Video content featuring illegal activity is not necessarily illegal itself - according to the Online Safety Act - it is up to the social network to de
body: Video content featuring illegal activity is not necessarily illegal itself - according to the Online Safety Act - it is up to the social network to decide whether flagged content is illegal and act accordingly.TikTok said its policies prohibit content that could cause significant physical harm, including dangerous driving.It added that it is actively removing videos and accounts that break its rules, including the account believed to belong to Saddington.The company said between January and March 2026, 99.8% of the content removed for violating those policies it took down proactively.While TikTok is taking some videos down, it is not necessarily because it has deemed them to be illegal - it may only be because they breach the firm's own terms and conditions.There are specific exceptions which are set out in the Online Safety Act, but they can be difficult to interpret.For example, content showing someone being killed is not necessarily illegal unless it is being shared by a terrorist group, and/or accessible to children.The BBC has also contacted Meta and X for comment.On Saturday, PC Tom Clough, 38, and PC Matthew Blades, 37, died when a Volkswagen Passat, which officers had been pursuing until seconds before, collided with their marked armed response car on the A66 near Middlesbrough.All five of the Passat's occupants - Saddington, Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jacob Matusiak, 23, Theo Rae, 17, and Cole Robert Worthy, 17 - also died.A video posted on the TikTok account believed to belong to Saddington in March 2025 showed him and four other young people involved in what appears to be a police pursuit. The video has since been deleted.BBC Verify analysed the 94 second-long clip, which showed the car driving on footpaths and parkland in Ormesby, Middlesbrough, with Saddington a rear-seat passenger.Another video posted by the same account, also since deleted, appears to show a joyride where a passenger is smoking, with the speedometer showing 100mph.Then, later in the video, a different car is set on fire. The passengers in this video are not identifiable.Cleveland Police and Crime Commissioner Matt Storey said: "Without being able to say whether that was anything like involved in this case, it's absolutely idiotic for anybody to be doing anything other than being completely 100% focused on the road when they're behind the wheel of a vehicle."He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that someone filming themselves or others driving dangerously is "absolutely ridiculous, and of course nobody should be doing that"."It is a worrying situation if that's becoming more prevalent because it is incredibly dangerous", he added.Earlier this month, five teenagers were killed in a head-on collision in County Kildare, Ireland, after driving the wrong way down a motorway.They hit a car which was believed to be carrying a family heading to the airport for a holiday. As of Friday, three women and a seven-year-old boy were still in hospital where they were being treated for serious injuries.At the time, Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly called it "irresponsible and dangerous driving".He said: "What makes this reckless behaviour even more appalling is that in some cases it is being done for social media likes regardless of the potentially devastating impact it might have on innocent people and themselves."Speaking to BBC Radio 5Live, Pollard said he wanted to see social media companies "step up".He added: "It's one of the reasons they've argued against some of the regulations, saying they can police themselves."Well this is the perfect opportunity to demonstrate it. Remove the content that celebrates dangerous behaviour on our roads."The minister said the government will use powers in the Online Safety Act to compel platforms to take down any content that remains online.A spokesperson for regulator Ofcom said under the act platforms "must minimise children's exposure to violent material and content promoting dangerous challenges".They added that in July, it launched an investigation "into TikTok's compliance with its child safety duties, and we've shown we'll take action if evidence suggests companies are falling short."

schema.headline: Sharing dangerous driving videos is 'truly reprehensible', PM says

title: Manchester Race Across the World star Jo Gardiner dies year after son
description: Image caption, Jo Gardiner travelled with her son Sam in the 2020 series of the BBC One showByGeorgie DockerNorth WestUpdated 2 hours agoA former Race
body: Image caption, Jo Gardiner travelled with her son Sam in the 2020 series of the BBC One showByGeorgie DockerNorth WestUpdated 2 hours agoA former Race Across the World contestant has died, a year after her son and co-star's death in a car crash.Jo Gardiner, 61, died "following a long and courageous battle with cancer", her family said.Gardiner, a physiotherapist from Manchester, travelled across South America with her son Sam in the second series of the BBC show, which aired in 2020.Her family said she was "one of a kind" who "lived fully, fiercely and never did anything by halves".Image source, PAImage caption, Jo Gardiner's family described her as "our joy, our safe place and our absolute treasure" Gardiner is survived by her son Charlie.Her son, Sam, who she appeared with on the show, died in June 2025 after his car came off the road and crashed. The mother and son competed on Race Across The World because Gardiner wanted to experience a travel adventure with Sam, who had ADHD.They competed against four other pairs of contestants racing from Mexico City down to Ushuaia in Argentina.'Outrageous spirit'Gardiner's family said "she had a rare gift for making everyone around her feel more alive"."She lived fully, fiercely and never did anything by halves," they added."She was blessed with countless friends, drawn to her extraordinary magnetism. "Somehow, each one felt as though they were among her very best."To us, she was more than all of these things. "She was our family, our joy, our safe place and our absolute treasure.""We know how deeply Jo was loved, and we take comfort in knowing that her laughter, her courage, her kindness and her wonderfully outrageous spirit will live on in the many people whose lives she touched."Image source, HandoutImage caption, Jo Gardiner was the "matriarch" of the Race Across The World family, producers sayThe family asked for privacy while they grieved, but urged "everyone who knew and loved Jo to do exactly what she would have wanted: tell the funny stories, raise a glass, have an adventure, laugh loudly and live life to the full".They said she was "one of a kind", adding: "There will never be another her."A Race Across The World spokesperson said: "On behalf of the Studio Lambert production team, the BBC and the whole Race Across The World cast, we offer our deepest and heartfelt sympathies to Jo's son Charlie, and her wider family and friends."Jo became the matriarch of the Race Across The World cast family, she leaves a lasting legacy in the many lives that she touched, both through the series and beyond. "It was a privilege to share her story and she will be deeply missed."Get in touchTell us which stories we should cover in Greater Manchester

schema.headline: Manchester Race Across the World star Jo Gardiner dies year after son

title: 'I didn't speak the Queen's English': Why people worry about their accents
description: Growing up in Manchester, Mia Tanswell didn't give her accent much thought - until her first week at university in Loughborough."I knew people were go
body: Growing up in Manchester, Mia Tanswell didn't give her accent much thought - until her first week at university in Loughborough."I knew people were going to notice that I was northern and that I didn't speak the 'Queen's English'," the 22-year-old says."Definitely in seminars I would sometimes feel like my accent would sound a bit less intellectual than other people, especially if I was the only northern student in the classroom."She's not alone. Fresh polling seen by the BBC suggests many workers still see so-called "accent bias" as a problem.The survey found one in 10 people in Britain feel anxious or self-conscious about their accent in high stakes professional settings such as speaking up in a business meeting.The research, conducted by the organisation More in Common of more than 3,300 adults across England, Scotland and Wales, found accent-related anxiety in work settings like these was highest among Geordies - from the region around Newcastle - and those with an east London - or Cockney - accent (at 19%), followed by people with a Welsh accent (at 18%).Around 5% of respondents believed their accent had cost them a promotion, pay rise or senior role. "Brummies" - people from Birmingham - were the most likely to feel this, at 13%.Respondents with a West Country accent reported the highest rate of having their accent mocked or criticised by colleagues, at 15%, followed by 13% of those with a Geordie accent.The poll was commissioned by Common Ground, an organisation which aims to promote social cohesion. Its founder, Lara Newman, has worked in construction, property and the built environment industry for more than 30 years, and says she changed her own accent to get ahead in the workplace."I am incredibly realistic about what would have happened had I gone to university or gone into the workplace with a strong west country accent," she says. "I felt like that was going to be an issue for me."Common Ground aims to support people from disadvantaged backgrounds into work but she says one of the layers creating a barrier to them is accent."I think there is a problem in the sense that [an accent] implies a level of education or otherwise. It implies class," she says.Most employers would say that is at least their ambition, to treat applicants and employees equally, regardless of their accent. Charlotte Davies, career expert at LinkedIn, says while there is still progress to be made "the direction of travel is encouraging"."Hiring is increasingly about skills, not background or polish. "Your accent is part of your story, and the workplaces getting this right, treat that as a strength, not something to smooth out," she says.Sian Jackson, a partner at law firm Mills & Reeve, says her company has recently changed its approach to encourage more local hiring and a diversity of accents."We don't judge, we scrutinise based on capability beyond somebody's accent, or appearance. Like any other prejudice or bias it's about being conscious of it so you can then set it aside," she says."We feel we've come a long way as a firm, but we are behind nationally compared to things like gender, so there is more progress to be made on accents."

schema.headline: 'I didn't speak the Queen's English': Why people worry about their accents

title: Dutch broadcaster Avrotros pulls out of  2027 Eurovision Song Contest
description: Dutch public broadcaster Avrotros has pulled out of next year's Eurovision Song Contest, saying that the competition can no longer be considered neutr
body: Dutch public broadcaster Avrotros has pulled out of next year's Eurovision Song Contest, saying that the competition can no longer be considered neutral while a participating country remains involved in a large-scale military conflict.In a statement, external released on Monday, the broadcaster said the decision was due to a lack of clarity from organisers - the Eurovision Broadcasting Union (EBU) - over assessing which countries could compete.Avrotros added: "The severe humanitarian suffering in Gaza and the ongoing restrictions on press freedom have contributed to increasing divisions surrounding the Eurovision Song Contest in recent years."Earlier this month, the EBU updated their rules to state that if a country involved in an armed conflict wins the competition, it will be ineligible to host it the following year. But Avrotros said those changes "do not provide sufficient confidence that ‌the ⁠independent and neutral character of the Eurovision Song Contest has been restored".The broadcaster's withdrawal from next year's contest in Burgas, Bulgaria, does not necessarily rule out Dutch participation.Another broadcaster within the Dutch public broadcasting system could potentially take it on as the country has several public broadcasters.Avrotros pulled out of this year's event in Austria, Vienna, which the Netherlands boycotted after Israel were allowed to compete.Only Ireland and Sweden have won Eurovision more than the Netherlands.Martin Green, director of the contest, said in a statement that the EBU regretted Avrotros's decision but respected its views. "We will now continue our dialogue with NPO, the umbrella organization for Dutch public service media, regarding the opportunities for another broadcaster to participate. We very much hope that audiences and artists in the Netherlands can continue to be represented in the Eurovision Song Contest."Taco Zimmerman, director general of Avrotos, said the Eurovision Song Contest "was originally created to bring people and countries together" but was now "a platform for division".  He said: "It is undeniable that international conflicts are increasingly affecting the contest, undermining its neutral character."The Eurovision Song Contest has therefore become a platform for division. As a public broadcaster, we remain committed to our values."He added: "They guide us in everything we do, even when that means stepping away from an event that is very close to our hearts. That is painful as we would have very much liked to be part of the contest again next year."Green, however, stated that the contest "has always been a place to bring people together, celebrate diverse communities, and show that a better world is possible even in the most difficult times".The NPO said it was "very sorry" to hear that the broadcaster had pulled out again, adding "we respect Avrotros's decision"."We also recognise that the geopolitical tensions are having a divisive effect," its response continued."That's why this hasn't been an easy decision for our colleagues. We will reflect on the upcoming edition and will come back to this at the right moment."The organisation concluded it was "too early to comment on the next steps at this point" and that its members were "currently deliberating on that".The recent amendment to the rules, that mean a country involved in an armed military conflict can't host the next contest if it wins, was approved by the contest's governing body, following feedback from participating broadcasters after Eurovision 2026.It stated that winning countries will also be disqualified from hosting if a "sensitive geopolitical situation" affects the "security, safety or stability of their state or immediate region".Last November, following a failed attempt to have Israel suspended, five broadcasters announced they were boycotting the competition - including Eurovision powerhouses Spain, Ireland and the Netherlands.Despite the protests, Israel's Noam Bettan ultimately took second place with his song Michelle.It marked the second year in a row that Israel had taken the runners-up position - and some participating broadcasters have privately expressed safety concerns over the contest being staged in Jerusalem or Tel Aviv, should the country win in the future.Although Israel will undoubtedly be seen as the target of the rule change, it will also affect Ukraine, which has been engaged in a protracted war since it was invaded by Russia in 2022.Ukrainian group Kalush Orchestra went on to win Eurovision that same year, in a symbolic show of public support.

schema.headline: Dutch broadcaster Avrotros pulls out of  2027 Eurovision Song Contest

title: Nearly three million Teslas recalled in China over hidden door handles
description: Minimalistic door handles became a signature feature of electric vehicles (EVs), but the controversial designs are now at the centre of China's bigges
body: Minimalistic door handles became a signature feature of electric vehicles (EVs), but the controversial designs are now at the centre of China's biggest car recall, affecting more than 4 million vehicles.The recall, which includes 2.98 million Chinese-made Teslas, follows safety concerns that the hidden door handles are difficult to locate and open in emergency situations.Other brands affected by the recall include Chinese carmakers XPeng, Xiaomi and Geely.The recalled vehicles will have a warning label stuck on the interior door and receive a software update to automatically lower the windows in a crash.The designs have come under scrutiny after two fatal crashes in China involving Xiaomi EVs, in which power failures were suspected to have prevented doors from being opened.Tesla said in a statement on Friday that it was recalling some of its Model 3, Y, S and X vehicles due to door handles that are "difficult to identify and operate because their colour is similar to the interior trim"."In extreme situations such as a severe collision causing the vehicle's low-voltage system to fail, this could hinder occupants from quickly opening the doors to escape and impede rescue efforts by those outside the vehicle, posing a safety hazard," it said.Tesla said it would place warning labels on the recalled vehicles and issue a software update to automatically lower a vehicle's windows after a collision.It is not clear if the affected firms plan to make a similar recall for the rest of the world.The BBC has contacted Tesla, XPeng, Xiaomi and Geely for comment.The use of hidden handle designs has "snowballed" after Chinese brands were quick to copy the "sleek" look of Tesla's Model S sedan since 2014, said Tu Le, the founder of consultancy Sino Auto Insights.The use of warning labels and a software update is more of a "band-aid" than a lasting solution for the issue, he added.In February, Chinese authorities announced a ban on hidden door handles.Under new rules due to take effect on 1 January 2027, cars will only be allowed to be sold in China if they have a mechanical release on both the inside and outside of their doors.Tesla's door handles were also involved in a probe by US safety regulators after reports that they suddenly stopped working, leaving children trapped in the cars.In July, the US National Highway Traffic Safety Administration suggested creating a new formal safety standard for all carmakers.The BBC has contacted the agency for comment.

schema.headline: Nearly three million Teslas recalled in China over hidden door handles

title: Yr Wyddfa rows between people queuing and those skipping the line
description: 'It's not Alton Towers' - rows break out over queuing at Wales' highest mountainFigure caption, One climber was told "there's a queue" when he reached
body: 'It's not Alton Towers' - rows break out over queuing at Wales' highest mountainFigure caption, One climber was told "there's a queue" when he reached the mountain summitByMatthew RichardsBBC WalesReporting fromYr WyddfaUpdated 7 hours agoVisitors to Wales' highest mountain are being urged to respect others by not skipping queues to reach the top following rows among climbers.Recent hot weather means there have been bumper summer crowds at Yr Wyddfa, also known as Snowdon, where people have reportedly waited more than one hour to reach the 1,085m (3,560ft)-high summit.Social media videos have shown arguments among queue-jumpers and those patiently waiting their turn to touch the metal plate that marks the top.A recent video showed Marc Screeton, from Manchester, being heckled as he bypassed the line, saying: "Imagine queuing on a mountain? No chance."But others have said queuing is necessary for safety reasons.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Queuing at places like Yr Wyddfa's summit is often an "unwritten and unspoken" rule, according to an expert in moral philosophyThe mountain's growing popularity in Eryri National Park, also known as Snowdonia, has led to bottlenecks, and queues are now common on the stone steps leading to a metal plate or trig point where people pose for photos and videos.Two charity hikers raising money for motor neurone disease were booed after skipping queues to reach the summit in May.Speaking to BBC Wales, walkers on the mountain had mixed views about those jumping the queues. Lucy Taylor said: "I think you should queue because it's really quite dangerous and everyone's trying to get up there - it's just not safe."Image source, BBC/Cwmni DaImage caption, One climber says people should realise they're "not at Alton Towers for a ride"Tina Millard from West Bromwich said: "I don't think that you should have to queue."It's a mountain, you should just be able to go up and that's it."We're not at Alton Towers for a ride. It's a mountain, it's for everyone," she said.Carl Lynch from Dunstable, Bedfordshire said: "It should be: 'go up there, two minutes and then move on for everyone else'. Simple as that."Throughout this year's hot weather national park wardens have urged visitors to follow the country code by leaving gates as they found them, taking their litter away with them and reducing the risks of wildfires.They have also urged people to wait their turn when queuing. Image caption, The trig point at the top of Yr Wyddfa is a common location for photo opportunitiesAlun Jones, an area warden for Eryri National Park Authority, urged those wanting to reach the trig point to be "considerate and don't skip the queue".While queuing is often not compulsory, it is often an "unwritten and unspoken" social contract, according to an expert in moral philosophy.Johann Go, who is also assistant professor of ethics at University College London, said: "So it's not that I have to queue, but given that others are already restraining themselves, if I were to then jump the queue, I would be saying 'to hell with them' and that my time is more valuable."Image source, Jamie RichardsonImage caption, Jamie Richardson (left) and Richard Thiedeman climbed Yr Wyddfa as part of the Three Peaks ChallengeIn May a pair of charity hikers were met with jeers from a queue at the summit as they tapped the trig point to complete a charity challenge.Jamie Richardson, 32, and Richard Thiedeman, 34, from Lincolnshire, were climbing Yr Wyddfa as part of the Three Peaks challenge to raise money for their friend who has motor neurone disease (MND)."I was getting booed and then there was a gentleman who was at the top, who had just had his photo taken and he physically tried to stop me," Richardson said. He said he had just touched the summit point and heard someone say "you should be ashamed of yourself".Richardson added: "There's no policing of it at all, it is purely free will, if you want to queue you can."The queuing, that is just purely down to British culture traditions."On social media, some described the scenes at the mountain over the May bank holiday weekend as having a carnival atmosphere due to the crowds there.Get in touchHave you been stuck in a queue on a mountain? Or do you refuse to wait in line?

schema.headline: Yr Wyddfa rows between people queuing and those skipping the line

title: Mother, grandmother and stepfather sentenced for 'house of terror' abuse
description: Image caption, Meaghann and William Murphy told how they were abused as young childrenByRebecca CurranBBC Scotland and Ken BanksNorth east Scotland re
body: Image caption, Meaghann and William Murphy told how they were abused as young childrenByRebecca CurranBBC Scotland and Ken BanksNorth east Scotland reporterReporting fromAberdeen Sheriff CourtUpdated 1 hour agoA mother, grandmother and stepfather who subjected three children to years of abuse in a "house of terror" have avoided jail. Shirley Freeman, Julia Stephen and David McColl's victims were beaten, starved and psychologically tormented between 2003 and 2012. Freeman, 51, and Stephen, 69, were earlier found guilty of cruel and unnatural treatment. McColl, 50, admitted the crimes. At Aberdeen Sheriff Court, Sheriff Craig Findlater said no sentence could "repair the awful childhoods" of the trio's victims. Warning: This article contains descriptions of child abuseTwo of their victims, William and Meaghann Murphy, who are now 25 and 28, told BBC Scotland News the violence and cruelty they experienced as children became their normal reality. Image caption, Shirley Freeman was found guilty of cruel and unnatural treatmentFreeman was sentenced to 18 months probation, 240 hours of unpaid work, and a 12-month restriction of liberty order, as a direct alternative to custody. Stephen was ordered to carry out 150 hours of unpaid work and given 18 months probation. And McColl was sentenced to 220 hours of unpaid work, 18 months probation, and an 11-month restriction of liberty order, as a direct alternative to custody.The abuse happened at an address in Balloch, Dunbartonshire, and at a flat in Aberdeen's Bedford Avenue.A trial heard that Freeman, now of Cullen, Moray, had created a "house of terror" for the children.Image caption, Meaghann Murphy said violence became normalised"The things that stick out for me were the anger, the violent outbursts that would come from my mother," Meaghann said."William and I were both locked in a room and because I was bursting for the toilet I had to take all my clothes out of my bottom drawer and use that."She went ballistic about it. I got slapped about for that. After that, instead of letting us out the room, she just put a bucket in the room."So my experience from the get-go has been just straight-up cruelty."She described being deprived of food for days at a time and said locks were placed on cupboards to prevent the children helping themselves.The court heard Freeman repeatedly struck the children with a metal-studded belt.Image caption, Meaghann and William would be looked in a room and were denied sleepWilliam said: "For as long as I can remember, family life was chaotic and unpredictable, and at times quite hostile. We were often made to sleep on the floor as a punishment."Sometimes when we had been really bad, they called it sleep deprivation, where they got us to stand up, like in a line, and we were made to stay awake."Your mind starts to play tricks on you. I remember starting to see faces in the wall."If we were dozing off or showed any sign that we weren't taking it seriously, things were thrown at us, or we were shouted at, and the punishment was then extended."He said his older sister tried to protect him.Image caption, William and his sister are now trying to get on with the rest of their lives"Meaghann was effectively like a human mattress," he recalled."She took the brunt of sleeping on the concrete, and she would then let myself cuddle into her and rub the back of my head."She tried to shield us from as much as possible. She was our protector."Meaghann said she continues to struggle with feelings of guilt over what happened, as she could not offer more protection."I'll live with it for the rest of my life," she said."I will never forgive myself for the things I had to see and I couldn't do anything about it."I know I was a child, but I didn't see it like that at the time and I still struggle to see it that way."By 2013, the siblings had both been taken in to care, amid child protection concerns.Police Scotland launched an investigation in 2022 after William made a statement.The siblings said they decided to speak out in the hope their story may help others."I feel like this is the first time we've ever really been given a platform that we can use to make a difference in some way," Meaghann said."Even if one person was to take something positive from it, then I've done my bit."William said he hoped sharing their experiences would help others recognise the signs of abuse.He concluded: "My mother, grandmother and stepfather are evil, barbaric and cruel."But it hasn't changed us. Not in the way they wanted it to anyway."'Horrific catalogue of mistreatment'Alison McKenzie, procurator fiscal for Grampian, Highlands and Islands, said the trio were adults when they "knowingly and deliberately subjected these children to a horrific catalogue of mistreatment".She said: "The evidence showed that, rather than providing the care, affection and security every child deserves, they engaged in a sustained pattern of cruelty, degradation and harmful behaviour."We hope this prosecution reassures others who have experienced child abuse that they will be listened to, treated with dignity and supported throughout the criminal justice process, regardless of when the offending took place."Det Insp Kerry McCombie, of Police Scotland, added: "The abuse spanned across the childhood years of the victims and I'd like to pay tribute to them for their bravery to bring this case before the courts."If you or someone you know have been affected by child abuse, you can find more details of help and support at the BBC Action Line. Get in touchWhat stories would you like BBC News to cover from NE Scotland, Orkney and Shetland?

schema.headline: Mother, grandmother and stepfather sentenced for 'house of terror' abuse

title: New Zealand moves to ban children under 16 from social media
description: New Zealand to introduce bill for under-16s social media banImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The proposed ban would apply to platforms like In
body: New Zealand to introduce bill for under-16s social media banImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The proposed ban would apply to platforms like Instagram, Snapchat and TikTokByAmy WalkerNew Zealand is to introduce a bill seeking to ban under-16s from using social media.Under the latest proposals, platforms including TikTok, Instagram, Snapchat and Facebook, will have to take steps to check users are over 16 and platforms that fail to meet their obligations could face fines of up to 10% of their global revenue.Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said social media was exposing children to "harmful content, addictive technology and pressures they are not equipped to deal with". But several political parties have said they will vote against the bill.The move follows a similar ban in Australia, while countries including the UK and Greece are set to introduce restrictions next year.Luxon said social media was affecting children's family life, mental health, sleep and education. "We have protections to keep children safe in the real world and we need them in the virtual world too," he said.New Zealand's government has not outlined which other "high risk" platforms could be impacted.A statement said that under the Online Safety Bill, which is being introduced to parliament on Monday, social media companies would be required to "take reasonable steps" to check users are over the age of 16 by using methods including existing account information, facial age estimation and digital identity checks.Platforms regularly used by children would also be required to regularly assess the risks they pose and report on how they are being identified and reduced.No penalties are proposed for children, parents or caregivers for breaches of the ban, but fines for social media companies could be substantially higher than in Australia, where the maximum penalty is $99m (£51.7m).It is unclear if the bill will get enough votes to pass however, after both the Act and New Zealand First (NZF) parties - which are coalition partners in the government - said they would oppose it.David Seymour, New Zealand's deputy prime minister and leader of Act, said the ban would not work.Foreign affairs minister Winston Peters, who leads the NZF party, said: "We have been concerned with the proposed legislation and the direction and slippery slope that legislation like this will inevitably take our country."Peters also described a ban introduced in Australia in December as a "colossal failure".The ban has been difficult for Australia to enforce, and it has been widely acknowledged that many children under the age of 16 have still been able to access and use banned apps.Earlier this month, France's top court struck down a similar proposed social media ban, saying it infringed upon freedom of expression.

schema.headline: New Zealand moves to ban children under 16 from social media

title: London Zoo animals hop on scales for annual weigh-in
description: Image source, PA MediaImage caption, All animal statistics, including those of Kiwi the Capybara, will be shared with keepers across the globeByRuth C
body: Image source, PA MediaImage caption, All animal statistics, including those of Kiwi the Capybara, will be shared with keepers across the globeByRuth ComerfordLondonUpdated 48 minutes agoAnimals at London Zoo are being checked and measured as part of its annual weigh-in day to monitor their health and wellbeing.Zookeepers will need to coax every bird, reptile, fish and  mammal - from the largest rodents in the world to the greenest katydids - to the weighing scale. Each measurement is added to the Zoological Information Management System (ZIMS), a global database shared with animal carers and conservationists that compares important information on thousands of endangered species.Many of the zoo's animals are trained to perch on a scale while zookeepers note down their measurements, but others will need to be tempted with a strategic snack.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Katydids are famous for their leafy green camouflage and loud mating callsAlthough the zoo houses more than 14,000 animals, the keepers will only have time to measure and log the weight of about 400 creatures.Daniel Simmonds, London Zoo's animal operations manager, said: "Regular weigh-ins help zookeepers track the health of our animals, including invertebrates like the magnolia land snails, the capybaras and Humboldt penguins, and genuinely help us manage the care of these animals, who play a vital role in our global conservation efforts."Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Humboldt penguins are listed as vulnerable in the wild due to threats such as climate change, overfishing and habitat disturbance.Among the animals weighed this year were capybara siblings Kiwi and Gizmo. Kiwi weighed in at 45kg (7st), while her brother Gizmo tipped the scales at 50.5kg (8st). While Giant Magnolia Land Snail No 2 weighed a modest 102.5g (3.6oz).Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Bolivian black-capped squirrel monkeys are native to Bolivia, Brazil and PeruImage source, PA MediaImage caption, The regular weigh-ins help zookeepers track the health of the zoo's creatures, including Vietnamese magnolia snails

title: Esports World Cup: AG.AL wins tournament in surprise victory
description: Though some players, commentators and fans have boycotted the EWC because of Saudi Arabia's involvement, it still proves popular.Organisers say the ev
body: Though some players, commentators and fans have boycotted the EWC because of Saudi Arabia's involvement, it still proves popular.Organisers say the event attracts 2,000 players from 100 countries, with some of the world's top esports stars among them.They claimed this year's EWC reached 850 million viewers across the tournament, with 175,000 tickets sold.Teams have previously told BBC Newsbeat they "can't afford to ignore" the contest and a potential share of its $75m (£50m) prize pot, as funding for esports is on the decline.The tournament is run by the Esports Foundation, which describes itself as a non-profit organisation. It was created with the support of the Saudi government, and the EWC launched with an announcement from Bin Salman.Investing in esports has been a part of the Kingdom's push to become a major player in global gaming - a strategy termed "pixelwashing" by website gamedeveloper.com, external.The country also recently acquired video game giant Electronic Arts in a record-breaking buyout.Critics claim it's an attempt to improve the country's international reputation and distract from complaints about its human rights record and anti-LGBT laws.Saudi Arabia has faced similar accusations of "sportswashing" due to its investments in football, golf and other sports - which it has spent years denying.

schema.headline: Esports World Cup: AG.AL wins tournament in surprise victory

title: SC Cambuur fans suffer burns and eye injuries after Feyenoord supporters throw fireworks
description: Feyenoord's general manager Robert Eenhoorn said he "cannot be happy" with their 5-2 victory in Leeuwarden, adding "frustration prevails too much for
body: Feyenoord's general manager Robert Eenhoorn said he "cannot be happy" with their 5-2 victory in Leeuwarden, adding "frustration prevails too much for that"."This problem obviously does not only affect Feyenoord and is unfortunately something we have been unable to put a stop to for decades," Eenhoorn said. "We will therefore have to sit down again with all stakeholders, clubs, the KNVB [Dutch football association], and the authorities to look for a solution together."Leeuwarden mayor Foort van Oosten also condemned the incident and promised an investigation, while the Dutch football association said it would revisit its protocols for incidents of disorder.The game resumed despite the injuries to the fans, but it would have been abandoned had a player or match official been hit."That doesn't feel right," Jan Bluyssen, the KNVB's manager of professional football competition affairs, told Dutch news agency ANP."We need to examine whether the protocol is still appropriate and how we might want to adjust it."

schema.headline: SC Cambuur fans suffer burns and eye injuries after Feyenoord supporters throw fireworks

title: Brydon Carse: What will it take to prevent England from more hangovers
description: Yet again, the England men's cricket team is picking through the wreckage of a late-night misdemeanour. The latest stain on the game's reputation is a
body: Yet again, the England men's cricket team is picking through the wreckage of a late-night misdemeanour. The latest stain on the game's reputation is a result of pictures of fast bowler Brydon Carse in handcuffs and surrounded by police officers outside a nightspot in Derby. His Durham team-mate Matthew Potts is in the images, while former England captain Ben Stokes appears in the background.If you're keeping score, we're now up to eight England players involved in incidents of this kind since Halloween last year.Harry Brook was punched by a nightclub bouncer in Wellington, with Jacob Bethell and Josh Tongue present. Ben Duckett was filmed drunk in Noosa, then Stokes and Gus Atkinson were there when a member of England's security staff was struck in a London nightclub in June, breaching a curfew in the process.To put it another way, there are 30 men currently on England central contracts. More than a quarter of them have been caught up in bother in the past 10 months. Of the four separate incidents, two have involved punches being thrown and another was a police matter.In Carse's case, the time spent in handcuffs came days after new England Test captain Joe Root called on his players to be "really good role models, good human beings".Root was speaking the day before England's first Test against Pakistan, for which Carse was part of the squad. The match was scheduled to still be ongoing when he found himself in the hands of the police.It is understood that Carse was not arrested. Both the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) and the Cricket Regulator will work to establish what happened. There are early suggestions he was denied entry back into a nightclub, or he had a drink poured over him.Carse was also not specifically on England duty at the time. He was released from the first-Test squad to play for Durham away at Derbyshire and was scheduled to report to Lord's for the second Test on Monday.As of Sunday evening, he remains part of the squad for the second Test. England will take time to gather some information before a decision on his involvement is made.Root warned his squad to "be adults" when he abolished the midnight curfew - in his first act as captain - that came into place after previous incidents. As part of that move, guidelines advising players about not drinking alcohol on the day before, during or after a game, or in public, have also been removed.There is a duty of care towards Carse. Two years ago, the 31-year-old was banned for historical betting offences and rebuilt his career to become an England regular in all three formats. No bowler has more Test wickets for England than Carse's 58 since he made his debut in October 2024.But there is also a deep sense of anger and frustration within the ECB at having to deal with another error of judgement by a high-profile player. Supporters will take their own view, among them a sense that the behaviour of these players is now beyond parody.Does someone have to be left out of a squad or given a meaty suspension for the penny to drop? This might be the opportunity for Root to stamp his authority on a new era.Naturally, there will once again be the debate about not denying players their freedom or stopping them from enjoying a victory.For Carse, a Saturday night out came less than 48 hours before he is scheduled to report for England. He is only a tweaked hamstring away from playing in a Test at Lord's on Thursday.Perhaps more damning is the kind of trouble this group of England players seem to find. Two punch-ups and a set of handcuffs. It also does not appear to have dawned on them that they are high-profile individuals, likely to attract attention, with footage finding its way to social media, as happened with Carse.And what about Stokes, who, despite being retired, remains an employee of the ECB via his central contract.As the former captain, should Stokes have been conscious about Carse being in that situation? What about the trouble in which Atkinson found himself alongside Stokes in June?Three weeks ago, Stokes denied the England team has a drinking culture, but rather that the game itself has a problem. What has Stokes done to distance himself or those around him from that drinking culture?Now there is a wait to see what happens next. The ECB only became aware of the incident on Sunday afternoon. The governing body will take a breath overnight and decide if Carse needs to be removed from the Test squad.Perhaps, on Tuesday, director of cricket Rob Key will once again explain why the players he manages cannot keep themselves out of trouble. In the aftermath of the Stokes-Atkinson incident in June, Key denied that England have become a "national embarrassment". He may be asked again.Key also might be asked about the whereabouts of new Test coach Stephen Fleming, who does not take up his post until the winter. Might Carse have been less inclined to step out of line had the new sheriff been in town?Well, here is another situation for England to manage. Only strong action will ensure there are no more.

schema.headline: Brydon Carse: What will it take to prevent England from more hangovers

title: How easy is it to find an NHS dentist? It depends on where you live
description: Cornwall, Devon and Northamptonshire have seen some of the biggest reductions in the number of practices offering NHS care. In Cornwall, more than a q
body: Cornwall, Devon and Northamptonshire have seen some of the biggest reductions in the number of practices offering NHS care. In Cornwall, more than a quarter of practices that previously offered NHS treatment have stopped doing so, making it one of the starkest examples of the shift away from NHS dentistry.The findings come as ministers have pledged to tackle so-called "dental deserts", but dentists say the current deal is not viable. Many have handed back their NHS contracts because to work is loss-making.In Somerset, fewer than one in five dental practices now offers NHS services. Alan, 83, who lives in the county, says he has given up trying to find an NHS dentist."I used to try, but getting a dental appointment anywhere near where I live would be impossible," he says.Alan has only one tooth remaining after the others "crumbled out over the years" and says he has had to adapt what he eats, although he jokes that he has perfected a way of eating Brazil nuts.Vivak Shah, who runs three dental practices in Northamptonshire, continues to offer NHS treatment but says it operates at a loss. He no longer takes on new NHS patients."Each year we struggle to decide what to do, and there is a limit to how much the private side can cover the NHS losses," says Shah.He warned that if practices stop providing NHS treatment, many patients could be left in pain or forced to seek help elsewhere in the health service, including hospital accident and emergency departments."A contract handed back in one town attracts little national attention on its own but repeated across the country for a decade it amounts to the quiet transformation of dentistry into a two-tier service," says Mark Dayan, head of public affairs at the Nuffield Trust."Access to dental care increasingly depends on what people can afford to pay and where they live."Jim Sykes is a dentist in Hexham. He handed back his NHS contract in 2024."It was a really hard emotional decision, but the NHS work was running at such a loss. I had to think of my team of staff and make it work," he says. Sykes asked if he could continue treating just children but was told he had to accept adults as well, or give up the NHS work."There has been a real breakdown in trust for me. Even if there was a new government offer, I would still be very nervous about entering a new NHS contract," he says.Sykes says that none of his friends in his graduating class in dentistry still works in the NHS. "My friends have gone private, retired or teach - any pathway to avoid NHS dentistry."Shiv Pabary, chair of the British Dental Association's General Dental Practice Committee, says the situation is "the direct result of choices made by successive governments". He warns that unless ministers "fix and fund NHS dentistry", more dentists could choose to reduce their NHS work or leave the service altogether.Overall dentist practice numbers have risen in England over the last decade."This is not a shortage of dentistry but a shortage of NHS dentistry," says Dayan. "Practices will need to be incentivised back into NHS work in the places where the NHS footprint has thinned most."While most parts of England recorded declines in practices offering NHS dental care, the reductions were smallest in North West London, the Black Country and North East London.North East London was the only area to see any increase during the period, recording one additional practice offering NHS treatment compared with a decade ago.Every other region of England saw the number of NHS dental practices fall.Looking at the number of practices doing NHS work is not the same as looking at exactly how much health service capacity there is - practices can vary in size. But if you look at other measures such as the amount of treatment being done, the numbers are still down, although not as steep as the fall in practice numbers.The government says that it is changing the dental contract and training more dentists in the areas most in need. The government says it will also make it a requirement for newly qualified dentists to practice in the NHS for a minimum period of at least three years.Campaign group 38 degrees calls the current dental crisis "shameful", with people being "forced to pay money they can't afford or suffer with the pain, shame, and further complications that come from being denied vital NHS healthcare".

schema.headline: How easy is it to find an NHS dentist? It depends on where you live

title: South Africa v New Zealand: Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu drops to bench
description: Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu has paid the price for an indifferent showing in South Africa's defeat by New Zealand, with the fly-half dropping to the ben
body: Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu has paid the price for an indifferent showing in South Africa's defeat by New Zealand, with the fly-half dropping to the bench for Saturday's rematch in Cape Town.The All Blacks, revitalised under new coach Dave Rennie, ran out 33-16 winners in the series opener in Johannesburg.Feinberg-Mngomezulu was turned over five times in possession and occasionally exposed in defence, before he shifted to full-back for the Springboks in the second half of Saturday's first Test.South Africa head coach Rassie Erasmus has recalled 32-year-old double Rugby World Cup winner Handre Pollard at 10, while injuries to Cheslin Kolbe and Grant Williams have brought Ethan Hooker and Cobus Reinach into the starting line-up at wing and scrum-half respectively.Siya Kolisi may return to the back row after recovering from a hamstring injury, but Erasmus has also named Paul de Villiers as a back-up at blindside flanker in case Kolisi is not ready.Thirty-nine year-old Deon Fourie, who came off the bench to play 77 minutes of the Springboks' 2023 Rugby World Cup final win over New Zealand, could win his first cap since that occasion after being named among the replacements."There were a handful of positives and negatives last week, but the main thing that let us down was that we created so many chances, but mistakes at crucial times cost us," said Erasmus."We'll put in a lot of work this week to ensure that we are sharp in that regard this weekend because if we had used even some of those chances, the result could have been completely different."South Africa side to face New Zealand: Willemse; Arendse, Kriel, De Allende, Hooker; Pollard, Reinach; Nche, Marx, Louw, Etzebeth, Nortje, Kolisi/De Villiers, PS du Toit, Wiese.Replacements: Fourie, Steenekamp, T du Toit, De Jager, Esterhuizen, Hanekom, Van den Berg, Feinberg-Mngomezulu.New Zealand may be tempted to give Richie Mo'unga an immediate Test return as they chase a 2-0 lead in the four-match series that has been marketed as 'Rugby's Greatest Rivalry'.The 32-year-old was first-choice stand-off during their 2023 Rugby World Cup campaign, but he has been ineligible for selection while playing his club rugby in Japan since.However, his signing for Canterbury and the Crusaders, along with an injury to Billy Proctor, has paved the way for his comeback.Mo'unga will start at 10 in Tuesday's match against Johannesburg-based provincial side the Lions.Mo'unga, who says his determination to return to Tests was fuelled by watching a Six Nations match while in a Japanese karaoke bar last year, is confident he can produce the form that earned him a spot in World Rugby's team of 2023."I'm competitive; I want to be the best," he said. "I know that there's a process to that, and at this point in time, the process looks a bit different around preparing someone else [All Blacks' current first-choice fly-half Ruben Love] to be the best."I'm really competitive, but I'm also a team man. Whoever gets the role, gets the role, and if it's not me, I'll do anything I can to help them succeed."This game was always coming for me. There was always going to be a return. I wasn't sure when it was, but mentally I've prepared for my return in the black jersey, and I'm ready."New Zealand side to face Lions: B Barrett; Fineanganofo, Ioane, Tavatavanawai, Narawa; Mo'unga, Hotham; Lauaki, Taukei'aho, Tosi, Darry, Tuipulotu, Sititi, Blackadder, Ta'eiloa.Replacements: Slater, Tu'ungafasi, Ma'u, Hannah, Lakai, Preston, Jacomb, Lienert-Brown.

schema.headline: South Africa v New Zealand: Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu drops to bench
